title: Physiological and psychological responses to tended plant communities with varying color characteristics
research_question: To examine the effects of colors in tended plant communities, particularly in terms of the physiological effects of different color combinations, proportions, and positions, on human physical and mental health.

participants.description: 40 undergraduates and postgraduates (20 men and 20 women), with an average age of 21.83 ± 2.72, from Shenyang, China. All were right-handed, with no mental illness, physical illness, or history of drug abuse.
participants.recruitment: University students (high efficiency and low cost)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 27 images of common types of tended plant communities in Shenyang, China, featuring combinations of yellow, green, and red foliage. The images focused on the middle ground (hedgerow and ball-shaped bushes) with manipulated color types, ratios, and positions. Stimuli included one-color (100% R, Y, or G), two-color (55%+45% combinations), and three-color (55% fixed + x% + (45-x)%) plant communities.

measures.instrument: Alpha wave activity (8–13 Hz) from electroencephalography (EEG)
Likert scale questionnaire (1-5 points for 'comfortable' and 'relaxed' statements)

mechanisms: Plant color directly impacts human senses, producing physical and mental reactions.
Alpha wave activity (8-13 Hz) is related to mental relaxation and calmness.
Green and yellow colors are associated with calm, comfort, and joy, while red is associated with arousal and uneasiness.
Color diversity in plant communities can enhance visual vibrancy and emotional health.
Specific color proportions and spatial distributions contribute to a sense of unity and balance, optimizing relaxation.
Warm colors (red, yellow) with high visibility may accelerate blood flow, increase blood pressure, and pulse, leading to irritability and nervousness.
implementation_implications: Future plant landscape design should consider rich plant colors.
Plant communities with two or three different colors are preferred over monochromatic ones for stronger physiological responses and positive ratings.
For three-color plant communities, the optimal color ratio for relaxation is 55% green + 25% yellow + 20% red, with green and yellow having the largest proportion and an even distribution.
Attention should be paid to the even distribution of color proportions in multi-layer plant communities.
In situations with a small number of plant colors, choosing green or yellow plants is beneficial for comfortable and relaxed environmental experiences.
Green + yellow and green + red combinations induce stronger relaxation effects compared with yellow + red combinations.

limitations: Subjects were undergraduates and postgraduates (18-27), limiting generalizability to the general public.
Stimuli depicted visual scenes from one particular climate with relatively monotonous plant color types.
Photoshop software was used for image processing and color recognition, which may be less accurate than MATLAB or Python.
Future research is needed to fully explore the effects of color proportion and position gradient.
Future research should investigate the effects of plant color on non-human animals, given their different visual perception abilities and needs.

paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Physiological and psychological responses to tended plant communities with varying color characteristics
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
AbstractExposure to plants has been reported to promote health and reduce stress, and plant color has direct impacts on physical and mental health. We used images of common types of tended plant communities in Shenyang, China, with combinations of yellow, green, and red foliage, as experimental stimuli. A total of 27 images were used as visual stimuli. We used electroencephalography to measure α wave activity (8–13 Hz) in 40 subjects while they viewed visual stimuli. These data were combined with subjective questionnaire data to analyze the relaxing effect of images of tended plant communities with different color types and proportions on people. The results revealed that, although there were slight differences between the electroencephalography and psychological findings, women were significantly more relaxed than men after viewing the images. Physiological and psychological responses varied with the types and proportions of colors in the tended plant communities: those of foliage with combinations of two or three colors induced stronger responses than images with a single color. Specifically, (1) for one-color plant communities, green or yellow plant communities induced a stronger relaxation effect than red plant communities; (2) for two-color plant communities, the optimal color proportion was 55% + 45%, and the green + yellow and green + red color combinations induced a stronger relaxation effect; (3) for three-color plant communities, the relaxation effect was strongest when the color proportion was 55% green + 25% yellow + 20% red. These data would provide a plant color matching in future plant landscape design, which may be helpful for creating healthy and relaxing environments.
